q-aa-comparison.label: Comparison with 'than'
q-aa-comparison.summary: Choose more or less by the contrast in the sentence; 'more than' can also mean 'beyond'.

q-aa-degree.label: Barely, hardly, merely, scarcely
q-aa-degree.summary: Barely, hardly and scarcely mean 'only just'; merely means 'only'. Choose by sense.

q-aa-iorto.label: Superior, inferior, senior, junior + to
q-aa-iorto.summary: Adjectives ending in -ior (superior, inferior, senior, junior, prior, anterior, posterior) are followed by 'to', never 'than'.

q-aa-absolute.label: Adjectives with no comparative/superlative
q-aa-absolute.summary: Perfect, complete, ideal, entire, universal, round, square, chief, excellent, supreme and similar words already name an extreme, so they take no 'more'/'most' and no -er/-est.

q-aa-anyother.label: Comparing one member against its own group
q-aa-anyother.summary: Comparing one member of a group with the rest of that same group needs 'any other': gold is more precious than any other metal (gold is itself a metal).

q-aa-double.label: Not 'more better' or 'most cleverest'
q-aa-double.summary: Never combine 'more'/'most' with an -er/-est ending on the same adjective.

q-aa-doubleneg.label: Seldom/never/hardly + a second negative word
q-aa-doubleneg.summary: Seldom, never, hardly, scarcely, rarely and barely already carry a negative sense, so the rest of the clause needs anybody/anything/any, not nobody/nothing/no.

q-aa-inversion.label: Subject-auxiliary swap after never/seldom/rarely
q-aa-inversion.summary: When never, seldom, rarely, scarcely or hardly opens a sentence on its own, the auxiliary verb moves in front of the subject, just as in a question.

q-aa-enough.label: Adjective/adverb + enough, not enough + adjective
q-aa-enough.summary: 'Enough' follows the adjective or adverb it modifies (brave enough, fast enough), and that word stays in its plain positive form.

q-aa-asverb.label: regard/describe/define need 'as'; elect/call/appoint refuse it
q-aa-asverb.summary: Regard, describe, define, treat, view and know take 'as' before the complement; name, elect, think, consider, call, appoint, make and choose take no 'as' at all.

rules.text: A contrast word (even though, although, but) tells you which way the comparison goes. If something 'looked workable' but was hard in practice, it was MORE complicated than expected, not less.
rules.ok: Though it looked simple, it was more complicated than expected.
rules.bad: Though it looked simple, it was less complicated than expected.

rules.text: 'More than + adjective' means 'beyond that': more than impressive = better than impressive. 'Other than' means 'different from', and 'rather than' needs a different pattern.
rules.ok: Her analysis was more than impressive.
rules.bad: Her analysis was other than impressive (= not impressive).

rules.text: Barely, scarcely and hardly all mean 'only just' (and are nearly negative); merely means 'only'; 'all but' means 'almost'. A sentence about falling behind needs 'barely / scarcely / hardly'.
rules.ok: Its systems could barely keep up.
rules.bad: Its systems could merely keep up.

rules.text: Adjectives ending in -ior — superior, inferior, senior, junior, prior, anterior, posterior — are followed by 'to', not 'than', to introduce the thing compared.
rules.ok: He is senior to me in the department.
rules.bad: He is senior than me in the department.

rules.text: Some adjectives already name a complete or extreme state and are not graded with 'more'/'most' or -er/-est: perfect, complete, chief, ideal, entire, universal, round, square, triangular, excellent, extreme, supreme, final, unique, impossible, eternal.
rules.bad: This is the most ideal solution.

rules.text: When one member of a group is compared with the rest of that very group, 'any other' (not just 'any') is needed to exclude the member itself from the comparison, since otherwise it is being compared with itself too.
rules.ok: Gold is more precious than any other metal.
rules.bad: Gold is more precious than any metal (gold is itself a metal).

rules.text: Never combine 'more'/'most' with an -er/-est ending on the same adjective: 'more better' and 'most cleverest' are both double comparatives/superlatives. Use one marker only.
rules.ok: He is the cleverest of all the officers.
rules.bad: He is the most cleverest of all the officers.

rules.text: Seldom, never, hardly, scarcely, rarely and barely already make the clause negative, so the rest of the sentence must use anybody/anything/anywhere/any, not a second negative word like nobody/nothing/nowhere/no.
rules.ok: He hardly knows anything about the matter.
rules.bad: He hardly knows nothing about the matter.

rules.text: When never, seldom, rarely, scarcely or hardly stands alone at the start of a sentence (with no 'than'/'when' partner later on), the auxiliary verb moves ahead of the subject, exactly as in a question: Never have I seen such courage; Seldom does he visit his village.
rules.ok: Seldom does he visit his village.

rules.text: 'Enough' is placed right after the adjective or adverb it modifies, never before it, and that adjective or adverb stays in its plain (positive) form, never comparative or superlative: brave enough, fast enough, not 'braver enough' or 'enough brave'.
rules.ok: She is wise enough to understand the risk.
rules.bad: She is enough wise to understand the risk.

rules.text: Regard, describe, define, treat, view and know take 'as' before their complement (regarded him as a brother). Name, elect, think, consider, call, appoint, make and choose take the complement directly, with no 'as' at all (elected him president, considered him the best).
rules.ok: I regard him as my own brother. They elected him the president of the club.
rules.bad: I regard him my own brother. They elected him as the president of the club.

q-aa-comparison.cue: A blank before 'complicated / impressive / ...' followed by 'than'.
q-aa-comparison.standard: Read the contrast in the sentence (workable on paper, nearly revelatory) and decide whether the second part is more or less.
q-aa-comparison.fast: If the clue says 'even though it looked X', the real result is the opposite of X.
q-aa-comparison.eliminate: Drop 'much' and 'rather', which do not fit before 'than' in this way.
traps: 'Much' and 'rather' sound natural but break the pattern with 'than'.

q-aa-degree.cue: 'could ___ keep up / afford / hear', where the blank is a degree adverb.
q-aa-degree.standard: Ask whether the sentence says 'only just' (barely, scarcely, hardly) or 'only' (merely).
q-aa-degree.fast: Fell behind or hardly managed = barely.
traps: Two options can be near-synonyms (barely, scarcely).
Merely sounds neutral but changes the meaning to 'only'.

q-aa-iorto.cue: An adjective ending in -ior (superior, inferior, senior, junior, prior) followed by a blank or 'than'.
q-aa-iorto.standard: Recognise the -ior ending and use 'to' in place of 'than'.
q-aa-iorto.fast: -ior + than is always wrong; -ior + to is always right.
q-aa-iorto.eliminate: Drop every option with 'than' once the adjective ends in -ior.
traps: 'Than' feels automatic after any comparison, but these specific words break that pattern.

q-aa-absolute.cue: more/most or an -er/-est ending placed before or after a word like perfect, complete, chief, ideal, round, unique.
q-aa-absolute.standard: Recognise the adjective as one that already names a complete state, then drop the comparative/superlative marker entirely.
q-aa-absolute.fast: Perfect, complete, ideal, universal, round, square, unique, impossible: never 'more', never '-er'.
q-aa-absolute.eliminate: Drop any option that adds 'more'/'most' or -er/-est to one of these words.
traps: 'More perfect' and 'most unique' are extremely common in speech but are not accepted in formal grammar.

q-aa-anyother.cue: One named member of a group compared with 'any' + the group's own category name.
q-aa-anyother.standard: Check whether the thing being compared is itself a member of the category named after 'than any'. If so, insert 'other'.
q-aa-anyother.fast: X is more Y than any [category X belongs to] -> add 'other' before the category.
q-aa-anyother.eliminate: Drop the option that leaves out 'other' when the compared item belongs to the same category.
traps: Missing that the subject of the sentence is itself a member of the group it is being compared with.

q-aa-double.cue: more/most appearing together with an adjective that already ends in -er or -est.
q-aa-double.standard: Keep only one degree marker: either 'more'/'most', or the -er/-est ending, never both.
q-aa-double.fast: more better, most cleverest, more wiser: always wrong.
q-aa-double.eliminate: Drop any option that keeps both markers on the same adjective.
traps: Doubling up for emphasis, which is common in speech but not accepted in formal grammar.

q-aa-doubleneg.cue: Seldom, never, hardly, scarcely, rarely or barely in the same clause as nobody/nothing/nowhere/no.
q-aa-doubleneg.standard: Recognise that the adverb already makes the clause negative, then switch the second negative word to its positive-sounding counterpart (anybody, anything, any).
q-aa-doubleneg.fast: Negative adverb already in the clause -> the rest of the clause needs any-, never no-/non-.
q-aa-doubleneg.eliminate: Drop any option that keeps a second no-/non- word alongside a negative adverb.
traps: 'Hardly ... nothing' sounds emphatic in speech but is a double negative in formal grammar.
'Rarely ... nobody' makes the same mistake with a different pair of words.

q-aa-inversion.cue: Never, seldom, rarely, scarcely or hardly at the very start of a sentence, with the subject and verb following in normal order.
q-aa-inversion.standard: Move the auxiliary verb (does/did/have/shall/will) to directly after the opening negative adverb, ahead of the subject.
q-aa-inversion.fast: Negative adverb first in the sentence -> auxiliary next, subject after that.
q-aa-inversion.eliminate: Drop any option that keeps the subject immediately after the opening negative adverb.
traps: This is easy to confuse with 'no sooner ... than' and 'hardly ... when', which also invert but need their fixed partner word too.

q-aa-enough.cue: 'Enough' placed either right before or right after an adjective/adverb, sometimes with a comparative ending.
q-aa-enough.standard: Put 'enough' immediately after the plain adjective or adverb; never place it before, and never use a comparative form with it.
q-aa-enough.fast: Adjective/adverb + enough, always in that order, always in the plain form.
q-aa-enough.eliminate: Drop any option with 'enough' placed before the describing word, or attached to a comparative like 'faster enough'.
traps: 'Faster enough' and 'bravest enough' wrongly combine a comparison with 'enough'.
'Enough brave' reverses the correct word order.

q-aa-asverb.cue: regard/describe/define/treat/view/know or name/elect/think/consider/call/appoint/make/choose followed directly by a complement, with 'as' present or missing.
q-aa-asverb.standard: Sort the verb into one of the two fixed lists, then add or remove 'as' accordingly.
q-aa-asverb.eliminate: Drop any option that adds 'as' after elect/call/appoint/consider, or drops 'as' after regard/describe/define.
traps: 'Considered as the best' and 'appointed him as lecturer' both wrongly add 'as' to a verb that refuses it.
'Regard him my brother' wrongly drops the 'as' this verb requires.

pyqs.text:
Select the correct option to fill in the blank.
The company expanded so quickly that its systems could ___ keep up.
pyqs.why: The systems fell behind the quick expansion, so they could 'only just' keep up: barely.

b.note: 'Merely' means only; it does not say the systems struggled.

c.note: 'Scarcely' also means only just and gives the same sense here; it is the closest rival to the key.

d.note: 'All but keep up' means 'almost keep up' and breaks the pattern 'could ___ keep up'.

pyqs.caution: 'Scarcely' fits just as well as 'barely' here. If an exam gives both, look for any other difference (usage or register); in this paper the printed key is 'barely'.

pyqs.text:
Select the correct option to fill in the blank.
Even though the plan looked workable on paper, executing it turned out to be ___ complicated than expected.
pyqs.why: 'Even though it looked workable' sets up a contrast: the real work was more complicated than expected.

a.note: 'Less complicated than expected' would not be a contrast with 'looked workable'; it would repeat it.

c.note: 'Much' would need 'much more' before 'than'.

d.note: 'Rather complicated than expected' does not form a comparison with 'than'.

pyqs.trick: Even though X looked easy, it was MORE hard.

pyqs.text:
Select the correct option to fill in the blank.
Her analysis was ___ than impressive; it was nearly revelatory.
pyqs.why: 'More than impressive' means beyond impressive, which fits 'nearly revelatory'.

a.note: 'Less than impressive' means not impressive, which clashes with 'nearly revelatory'.

c.note: 'Other than impressive' means different from impressive, which would mean not impressive.

d.note: 'Rather than impressive' is not a comparison of degree.

practice.text:
Select the correct option to fill in the blank.
The task looked easy, but doing it was ___ difficult than we had imagined.
practice.why: 'Looked easy, but' signals the opposite: more difficult than imagined.

a.note: 'Less difficult' would repeat the idea of 'easy' rather than contrast with it.

c.note: 'Much' needs 'more' to make a comparison with 'than'.

d.note: 'Rather' cannot be used with 'than' to compare the degree here.

practice.text:
Select the correct option to fill in the blank.
The old man was so tired that he could ___ lift his bag.
practice.why: So tired that he could 'only just' lift it: barely.

a.note: 'Merely' means only and drops the sense of struggle.

c.note: 'All but' means almost and cannot sit between 'could' and the verb.

d.note: 'Just as' begins a comparison; it is not a degree adverb here.

practice.text:
Select the correct option to fill in the blank.
Her answer was ___ than correct; it was brilliant.
practice.why: 'More than correct' means beyond correct, which suits 'brilliant'.

b.note: 'Less than correct' means not quite correct, which clashes with 'brilliant'.

c.note: 'Other than correct' means not correct.

d.note: 'Rather than correct' is not a degree comparison.

practice.text:
Select the correct option to fill in the blank.
As the elder brother, he is naturally senior ___ me in the family business.
practice.why: 'Senior' ends in -ior and is followed by 'to', never 'than'.

a.note: 'Senior than' is one of the commonest errors with -ior adjectives; the correct word is 'to'.

c.note: 'Senior from' is not a standard construction.

d.note: 'Senior over' is not a standard construction.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
He is / junior than / most of his colleagues / in experience.
practice.why: 'Junior' is an -ior adjective and takes 'to', not 'than': it should be 'junior to most of his colleagues'.

c.note: A correct noun phrase, once the preposition before it is fixed.

d.note: A correct closing phrase.

practice.text:
Select the correct option to fill in the blank.
After the long renovation, the old palace looked almost ___ again.
practice.why: 'Perfect' already names a complete state and takes no comparative or superlative marker.

a.note: 'More perfect' doubles a degree the word 'perfect' already carries by itself.

c.note: 'Most perfect' makes the same mistake with the superlative marker instead.

d.note: 'Perfecter' is not a recognised word at all.

practice.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
The architect called it [[the most ideal]] design for a small flat.
practice.why: 'Ideal' already names a best-possible state, so it takes no comparative or superlative marker at all.

b.note: This repeats the original error unchanged.

c.note: 'More ideal' still wrongly grades a word that is not graded.

d.note: 'Idealest' is not a recognised word.

practice.text:
Select the correct option to fill in the blank.
The Ganga is longer than ___ river in the country.
practice.why: The Ganga is itself a river, so 'any other river' is needed to exclude it from the group it is being compared with.

a.note: 'Any river' wrongly includes the Ganga itself in its own comparison.

c.note: 'All other' does not fit the singular comparison pattern 'longer than ...'.

d.note: 'The other' implies there are only two rivers being compared, which the sentence does not say.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
Everest is / higher than any / mountain in / the Himalayan range.
practice.why: Everest is itself a mountain in that range, so the comparison needs 'any other mountain', not just 'any mountain'.

c.note: A correct noun phrase, once 'other' is added before it.

d.note: A correct closing phrase.

practice.text:
Select the correct option to fill in the blank.
This year's monsoon has been ___ than last year's.
practice.why: 'Worse' is already the comparative of 'bad'; adding 'more' in front doubles the degree marker.

a.note: 'More worse' combines 'more' with the comparative 'worse', which already carries the comparison.

c.note: 'More bad' is not how the comparative of 'bad' is formed; it is 'worse'.

d.note: 'Most worse' mixes a superlative marker with a comparative form.

practice.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
She is [[the most cleverest]] student in the entire batch.
practice.why: 'Cleverest' is already the superlative; adding 'most' in front doubles the degree marker.

b.note: This repeats the original error unchanged.

c.note: 'More cleverest' still combines a degree marker with an ending that already carries the comparison.

d.note: 'The most clever' is a correct superlative on its own, but it changes the given form more than necessary when 'the cleverest' is available and matches it exactly.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
The old watchman / rarely saw / nobody near / the warehouse at night.
practice.why: 'Rarely' already makes the clause negative, so the rest needs 'anybody', not a second negative word 'nobody'.

a.note: 'The old watchman' is a correct subject.

b.note: 'Rarely saw' is a correct negative-adverb verb phrase.

d.note: 'The warehouse at night' is a correct closing phrase.

practice.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
He hardly knows [[nothing]] about the new software.
practice.why: 'Hardly' already carries a negative sense, so the rest of the clause needs 'anything', not another negative word.

b.note: This repeats the original error unchanged.

c.note: 'Something' would mean he does know a little, which reverses the intended meaning.

d.note: 'No things' is not a standard English phrase and still doubles the negative.

practice.text:
Select the correct option to fill in the blank.
Seldom ___ such dedication among new recruits.
practice.why: A negative adverb opening the sentence on its own forces the auxiliary 'do' ahead of the subject 'we'.

a.note: The subject is placed before the verb, as in a normal statement, which is not allowed after an opening negative adverb.

c.note: This keeps the normal word order and also changes the tense needlessly.

d.note: This changes the tense without fixing the missing inversion.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
Never I have / witnessed such / chaos at a / railway station before.
practice.why: After the opening 'Never', the auxiliary 'have' must come before the subject 'I': 'Never have I witnessed...'.

b.note: 'Witnessed such' is a correct continuation once the inversion is fixed.

c.note: 'Chaos at a' is a correct continuation.

d.note: 'Railway station before' is a correct closing phrase.

practice.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
He is [[enough strong]] to lift that heavy box alone.
practice.why: 'Enough' is placed right after the adjective it modifies, in its plain form: 'strong enough'.

b.note: This repeats the original error unchanged.

c.note: 'Stronger enough' wrongly combines a comparative form with 'enough', which needs the plain form.

d.note: 'Enough strength' turns the adjective into a noun and still places 'enough' in the wrong position.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
She is / fastest enough / to qualify for / the state championship.
practice.why: 'Enough' follows the plain form of the adjective, not the superlative; it should read 'fast enough'.

c.note: 'To qualify for' is a correct continuation.

d.note: 'The state championship' is a correct closing phrase.

practice.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
The committee [[considered him as]] the most suitable candidate for the post.
practice.why: 'Consider' takes its complement directly, with no 'as': 'considered him the most suitable candidate'.

b.note: This repeats the original error unchanged.

c.note: Moving 'as' before the object does not remove the error; 'consider' still refuses 'as' anywhere in this pattern.

d.note: 'To be as' adds extra words and still keeps the unwanted 'as'.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
The teacher always / regarded him his best / student and / praised his sincerity.
practice.why: 'Regard' requires 'as' before its complement; it should read 'regarded him as his best student'.

a.note: 'The teacher always' is a correct opening.

c.note: 'Student and' is a correct continuation once 'as' is added.

d.note: 'Praised his sincerity' is a correct closing phrase.
